strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem with an identifiable audience in machine learning for code and reverse engineering. Transferring information from source code and comments into an encoder that subsequently consumes only the low-level representation is a worthwhile research direction.

The evaluation covers four downstream tasks and reports promising improvements. Function-name accuracy reaches 33.41 versus 29.41 for the strongest reported baseline, and summarization BLEU-4 reaches 34.36 versus 32.43. These findings could be useful without requiring state-of-the-art performance.

Figure 2 and Algorithm 1 communicate the overall training pipeline reasonably well. The comment-removal and encoder-freezing ablations provide useful initial evidence about design choices, and the manuscript reports dataset counts and several fine-tuning settings.
weaknesses: Necessary—align the claims with the evaluated input representation. Sections 3.1–3.2 obtain LLVM IR directly during compilation, rather than lifting stripped executable binaries. Figures 7–8 retain informative function and type names. Compiler-generated LLVM IR is not trivially interchangeable with stripped machine code, contrary to footnote 1. The results therefore support a narrower LLVM representation-learning claim; broader binary-analysis claims require an appropriate evaluation and a documented preprocessing pipeline.

Necessary—resolve the POJ-104 task definition. Section 3.2 and Table 2 specify disjoint sets of 64 training, 16 development, and 24 test problem labels, while Section 4.2 describes classification into 104 classes. Ordinary supervised classification does not explain prediction of these unseen classes. If the experiment is actually similarity retrieval, specify the training objective, candidate pool, ranking procedure, and evaluation cutoffs. MAP, MAR, and MAF1 also need precise definitions. This ambiguity prevents a reliable interpretation of Table 3 and the ablations that reuse this task.

Necessary—make the implemented method reproducible. Equation 4 omits the softmax stated in the surrounding text; an average of Gram matrices is not generally a valid probability target for the cross-entropy in Equation 5. Specify target normalization, whether gradients pass through targets, loss direction and reduction, and any embedding normalization or temperature. The encoder checkpoints, tokenization and pooling, actual interpolation-network architecture, and downstream generation decoder are also insufficiently specified. Referring to SimpleCLIP settings does not resolve these choices.

Necessary—separate the interpolation contribution from additional training. CONTRABIN-PCL receives 10 pretraining epochs, whereas the full model receives 30 or 70 depending on the downstream task. The interpolation-removal ablation again receives only 10 epochs. The assertion that it converged does not establish that the improvement comes from interpolation rather than the additional optimization or changed schedule. A comparison with matched training budgets is needed for this attribution, and the individual benefits of scalar versus feature-wise interpolation remain unisolated. Alternatively, narrow the conclusions to the observed performance of the complete pipeline.

Necessary—clarify the held-out evaluation and data provenance. Section 3.2 states that generation performance is evaluated on validation data, while the surrounding discussion also refers to an AnghaBench test set inherited from pretraining. Identify exactly which partitions produced Tables 5–6, how checkpoints and settings were selected, and how the pretraining holdout was divided for downstream learning. Document overlap and duplicate handling across the GitHub-derived corpora. The current description does not establish an unambiguous independent evaluation protocol.

Necessary—limit semantic-comprehension claims to what the evaluation measures. Section 3.1 generates comments with CodeT5; explicitly identify whether these also supply the summarization references and assess their quality. Agreement with generated references does not itself establish semantic faithfulness or human usefulness. Likewise, BLEU, GLEU, and exact match measure textual reconstruction rather than behavioral correctness of generated programs. Selected examples do not close this gap; Figure 8 even displays an incomplete shift expression in both reference and generated code. Claims of semantic consistency require suitable correctness evidence, or should be narrowed to the reported lexical metrics.

Necessary—correct the interpretation of the embedding visualization and calibrate performance claims. Section 4.1 incorrectly argues that unique programs should not cluster: distinct programs can share semantic properties, and separate t-SNE plots do not prove improved embedding geometry. Treat Figure 6 as illustrative. Also, Table 6 shows lower reverse-engineering BLEU-4 than GraphCodeBERT, 71.14 versus 71.56, and only a 0.43 percentage-point exact-match advantage. With single-seed results and no uncertainty estimates, broad claims of considerable, robust improvement need qualification or additional evidence.

Optional—improve editorial consistency after resolving the substantive issues. Correct the repeated three-versus-four-task descriptions, inconsistent DIRE/DIRT/DIRTY naming and references, GLUE/GLEU terminology, and the reference to Figure 7 for the Table 7 ablation results. More concise treatment of the human-learning analogy would also make the experimentally supported contribution easier to identify.
